subject: geography
title: Theories of Power and Future World Orders
welcome_lead: Trace the intellectual frameworks that explain how power has been won, held, and lost.
meta_desc: A-Level Geography Superpowers: Wallerstein world systems, Modelski cycles, multipolarity.
final_note: You have grasped the longue duree of global power transitions.

concepts.def: Wallerstein: core, semi-periphery and periphery zones.
Wealthy industrial states dominating global trade.
Low-income states supplying raw materials and labour.
Modelski: ~100 year rise and fall of dominant powers.
Power distributed among several competing states.
Indirect control of poorer states via economic ties.

walkthroughs.body_html: Immanuel Wallerstein's World Systems Theory divides the global economy into three zones: core (USA, EU, Japan) extracting surplus value, semi-periphery (China, Brazil, India, Russia) industrialising and mobile, and periphery (sub-Saharan Africa, parts of Latin America) supplying raw materials. China's transition from periphery to semi-periphery and now toward core status represents the most dramatic upward mobility in modern history.

George Modelski identified ~100-year hegemonic cycles: Portugal (16th C), Netherlands (17th C), Britain (18th-19th C), USA (20th-21st C). Each cycle has four phases: world war, world power, delegitimation, deconcentration. Some analysts argue the USA entered delegitimation after 2008, with China positioning for a deconcentration phase by 2030.

Three futures are debated. Bipolarity: US-China rivalry mirrors the Cold War. Multipolarity: USA, China, EU, India and Russia balance one another. G-Zero (Ian Bremmer): no power leads, producing chaos, weak global governance and rising regional powers like Turkey, Iran, Saudi Arabia. Climate change, AI and pandemics test all three models.

mcqs.q: Which zone in Wallerstein's model supplies raw materials?

numericals.q: Approximately how many years does a Modelski hegemonic cycle last?

free_texts.q: What term describes power distributed among several competing states?
